newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar call options in high demand - Tokyo dealers.
newsitem.headline: Dollar call options in high demand - Tokyo dealers.

text.p: Growing expectations that the Group of Seven (G7) nations are unlikely to hammer out specific measures to reverse the recent strength of the dollar are keeping dollar call options in high demand, dealers said.

"People had expected the dollar/yen spot rate to be range-bound until the G7 meeting, but recent remarks by officials on both sides of the Pacific spurred fresh dollar buying in spots as well as options," said Takashi Fujieda, chief options dealer at Yasuda Trust and Bank.

Prime minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on late Monday expressed doubts about the possibility of lowering the value of the dollar while U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated that a strong dollar is in the U.S. interest.
Both comments convinced options traders that the G7 nations may call for the stability in the currency market rather than showing strong concerns about the dollar's rise.
Finance ministers and central bank governors of the G7 nations will gather in Berlin on Saturday.

On Tuesday in Tokyo, there was active buying of dollar call options worth a few billion dollars from overseas operators, probably U.S. funds. This apparently caused a substantial amount of delta hedge buying on a spot basis by bankers and lifted the spot dollar rate against the yen.
Dealers said these options carried a life of six months to one year with strike prices of between 130 and 135 yen.

There was also a rumour that one-month call options with strikes of 131 yen were traded in London on Tuesday, dealers said. The dollar/yen risk reversal, which shows the pricing differential between puts and calls, favoured dollar calls at around 0.5/0.8 percent in the one-month, up from 0.3/0.7 on Tuesday.
The dollar/yen risk reversal had been long in favour of dollar puts because of persistent dollar selling interest by Japanese exporters.
"There was relatively stronger demand for longer-term calls on Tuesday, but the demand was spreading out to short-dated ones today," said Yasuda Trust's Fujieda.

Takeshi Uchida, product manager of currency options and derivatives at National Westminister Bank in Tokyo, said: "Recent high demand for longer-term calls may reflect the fact that operators are having more confidence in the dollar's strength over the long term," he added.
"The market is factoring into a spot dollar/yen rise to 125 yen (after the G7 meeting)," he added.
The dollar hit 123.18 yen in Tokyo on Wednesday, its highest in nearly four years.
In the wake of the rise in the spot dollar/yen rate, options volatilities has also surged.

One-month dollar/yen options volatility soared to around 13.00/40 percent in afternoon Tokyo, its highest level since late 1995, options dealers said. It was at around 11.9 percent on Monday. One-year rose to 12 percent in late trade, up from 11.80 percent from morning trade.

Uchida said if there is no specific accord to lower the value of the dollar at the G7 meeting, the one-month volatility may reach to around 15 percent in tandem with spot dollar's rise to 125 yen. But the speed of a rise in the volatility may slow down as operators are expected to cash in profits on further rises.
